claims.text: Tribo-induced rupture of the passive oxide film is the dominant mechanism governing synergistic degradation during simultaneous wear and corrosion in high-entropy alloys.
Appropriate recrystallization heat treatment homogenizes the microstructure of a Cantor-type alloy and restores corrosion resistance.
The proposed starting alloy has a uniform, well-established passive oxide film.
Separate inert-electrolyte wear, static NaCl corrosion, and sliding-in-NaCl tests provide a controlled comparison of isolated and coupled degradation.
Increasing mechanical load or sliding speed modulates the extent of oxide-film disruption.
The integrity of the passive oxide film is the structural mediator of the coupled response.
Sliding contact mechanically disrupts or thins the protective oxide film.
Film disruption exposes a less-passivated alloy substrate and accelerates localized corrosion.
Accelerated corrosion weakens the surface and thereby increases the wear rate.
The feedback between film rupture, corrosion, and wear causes total tribocorrosion degradation to exceed the additive effects of separately measured wear and corrosion.
Total degradation under tribocorrosion will significantly exceed the arithmetic sum of degradation from pure wear and static corrosion.
Increasing load or sliding speed will disproportionately increase wear damage and wear rate.
Increasing load or sliding speed will disproportionately increase corrosion rate under tribocorrosion.
Grain size and microstructural state can change oxide cracking and wear resistance in CoCrFeMnNi.
Alloy composition can alter passive-film stability and corrosion resistance.
The mechanism should apply when the alloy has a robust but mechanically sensitive passive film that sliding can disrupt.
The mechanism may fail when the passive layer is inherently unstable, rapidly regenerable, or exposed to environments in which film rupture is not the sole mediator.

Failure of tribocorrosion degradation to exceed the sum of isolated wear and corrosion, or observation of an intact film across the tested loads and speeds, would falsify the dominant-film-rupture hypothesis.
